The platform was developed by a research group led by Gao Caixia at the Institute of Genetics and Developmental Biology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

more.title: Local protein supply chain keeps nerve cells' mitochondria in check
more.summary: Some tracers used in hospital scans to check what is happening inside a patient's body are so short-lived they must be made on demand on site or rushed in by courier. A new study led by Angelika Harbauer's group at the Max Planck Institute for Biological Intelligence shows that nerve cells use similar strategies to deliver a protein that checks for damage in their mitochondria, the tiny structures that supply…

more.title: Sex in Britain has changed significantly, especially among young people
more.summary: The sex lives of people in Britain have shifted markedly since 1990, and their sexual and reproductive health needs are substantial and varied, according to the fourth National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal-4). The first five papers from the survey—one of the largest studies of sexual behavior in the world—are published in The Lancet.

more.title: Microplastics in nearly 8 in 10 fish sampled off Oman's Sohar coast
more.summary: Researchers at Sultan Qaboos University detected microplastics in the gills or digestive tracts of 95 of 120 fish sampled off Sohar in the Sea of Oman. Published in Scientific Reports, the study provides a baseline for tracking microplastic pollution in fish along this stretch of Oman's coast.

more.title: Ultrathin 'rainbow' sails could power spacecraft and shade the Earth
more.summary: For years, whimsically minded space enthusiasts have been dreaming of sailing across the vastness of the void on beams of sunlight. Photons, the massless particles that make up those beams of sunlight, still carry momentum and can therefore impart a gentle push when they bounce off a surface.

more.title: Carbon-rich soil near old oaks does not attract more earthworms, study finds
more.summary: Solitary oaks in traditional Romanian wood pastures create islands of carbon-rich soil around their trunks. However, a research team led by the Universities of Göttingen and Hildesheim found this does not mean more earthworms. In traditional wood pastures in Romania, the topsoil near the trunk held about a third more organic carbon and a quarter more nitrogen than the open grassland, yet earthworm numbers were no…

more.title: Amateur Astronomer? Be a Kilonova Catcher!
more.summary: Neutron stars are the ultra-dense, city-sized leftovers of dead stars. When they collide, they can release a brief flash of light called a kilonova. These immensely powerful events forge much of the universe’s gold, platinum and other heavy elements. Since a kilonova fades within days, astronomers have to find it fast, and no single observatory […]

more.title: Quantum blueprint maps a practical path to testing unusual entanglement
more.summary: Adrian Del Maestro knows how to engineer a quantum fingerprint. Rick Mukherjee has a gift for tuning atoms. Their combined expertise has taken a theory sketched out on paper and created a pathway for real experiments. The results, published in the journal Physical Review Letters, move a law-defying "mathematical oddity" ever so slightly up the technology readiness scale

more.title: Flowers in Renaissance sculpture may reveal political ambitions of Florence's ruler
more.summary: A new study suggests that the flowers adorning Benvenuto Cellini's sculpture Narcissus are more than decoration: they connect the development of botanical science with competition among Renaissance artists and the ambition of Florence's ruler to consolidate his status.

more.title: A new reason for magic numbers: Scientists discover the secret behind an unusually stable molecular cluster
more.summary: Why are some groups of molecules remarkably stable while others readily break apart? Researchers at Bar-Ilan University have discovered a surprising explanation for why clusters containing exactly six molecules of glycine, the simplest amino acid, are exceptionally stable—making six a "magic number." Moreover, they have uncovered the reason for this increased stability.

more.title: A black hole the size of an atom could destroy an entire star
more.summary: MIT scientists have discovered that tiny black holes left over from the Big Bang could slowly devour stars from within, eventually triggering spectacular explosions visible across galaxies. Detecting these unusual cosmic events could reveal the existence of primordial black holes and help solve the mystery of dark matter.

more.title: Blind sample test reveals how BepiColombo could decode Mercury's mineral makeup
more.summary: An international team of researchers, including scientists from Planetary Science Institute (PSI), has demonstrated that instruments aboard the BepiColombo spacecraft can operate together to identify the minerals that make up Mercury's surface, addressing a longstanding challenge in planetary science.

more.title: NASA’s Titan-Bound Dragonfly Rotorcraft Gets Its Eyes
more.summary: Science instruments for NASA’s Dragonfly are starting to arrive at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) in Laurel, Maryland, where the car-sized rotorcraft is coming together for its mission to explore Saturn’s largest moon, Titan. First to check in: DragonCam, which consists of seven cameras designed to characterize Titan’s surface at multiple scales during […]

more.title: Half of NASA's aging Mars fleet knocked offline by technical issues
more.author: Stephen Clark
more.summary: Perseverance is having trouble transmitting to Earth. Odyssey is rapidly burning through its waning fuel supply.

more.title: Mitsubishi Electric Research Lab CEO on How He Reached the C-Suite
more.author: Kathy Pretz
more.summary: The trajectory from researcher to top executive at a leading R&D organization doesn’t happen overnight. It took Anthony Vetro nearly 30 years to climb the corporate ladder at Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories , in Cambridge, Mass. He joined MERL in 1996, right out of college, and he has worked there ever since.

more.title: How brewers can protect beers from smoke-tainted hops
more.author: Jennifer Ouellette
more.summary: Study: Brewers can still use up to 50% of smoke-tainted hops without affecting beer taste and aroma.

more.title: New EU Bureaucracy Index: EU law has more than doubled since 2010
more.summary: The new EU Bureaucracy Index measures the volume of EU law in force, and it shows a record high: At the end of 2025, the EU regulations and directives in force comprised around 47,600 standard pages, 118% more than in 2010. The volume of EU law has thus more than doubled in 15 years, and it continued to grow in 2025.

more.title: Queensland keeps learning disaster lessons. So why do we keep forgetting them?
more.summary: After an early start to Queensland's storm season, with severe storms and flooding already affecting communities across the state, attention is once again turning to disaster preparedness and response.

more.title: Hurricane season wrap-up: El Niño fueled record number of Pacific storms but calmed Atlantic
more.summary: The 2026 hurricane season, which officially ends on Nov. 30, will be remembered as a year of contrasts between the Atlantic and Pacific, a classic indication of a hurricane season influenced by a very strong El Niño. Below-normal activity across the Atlantic basin was offset by above-average activity in the Pacific, including two disasters in Hawaii.

more.title: Ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side rewrite the Solar System’s violent past
more.summary: Scientists studying ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side have uncovered surprising evidence that challenges decades of thinking about the Solar System’s violent past. Instead of a single catastrophic bombardment, asteroid impacts appear to have declined gradually over billions of years, revealing new clues about Earth's early evolution and the origins of life.

more.title: Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it
more.summary: Scientists have uncovered surprising evidence that Earth’s next ice age may have already begun, only to be stopped by global warming. By studying ancient plants preserved beneath the Barnes Ice Cap in the Canadian Arctic, researchers discovered that the remnants of a massive ice sheet began expanding again about 2,000 years ago, signaling the possible start of a new glacial period.
